title: Signals & Their Properties
description: Continuous and discrete signals, periodicity, symmetry, energy and power, and time transformations.

study.title: Continuous and discrete time
study.body: A continuous-time signal $x(t)$ is defined for every real $t$; a discrete-time signal $x[n]$ only for integer $n$. Sampling a continuous signal every $T_s$ seconds gives a sequence. A sinusoid $\cos(\omega t)$ becomes $\cos(\Omega n)$ with $\Omega = \omega T_s$ in rad/sample.

study.title: Periodic signals
study.body:
$x(t)$ is periodic if $x(t+T) = x(t)$ for all $t$; the smallest such $T>0$ is the **fundamental period** $T_0$. A sum of sinusoids is periodic only if every ratio $T_1/T_2$ is rational; then $T_0$ is the least common multiple of the periods (equivalently, $\omega_0$ is the greatest common divisor of the frequencies).
**Discrete time:** $\cos(\Omega_0 n)$ is periodic only if $\Omega_0/2\pi = m/N$ is rational; in lowest terms $N_0 = N$.

study.title: Even and odd parts
study.body: Even: $x(-t) = x(t)$ (mirror image about $t=0$). Odd: $x(-t) = -x(t)$, so $x(0)=0$. Every signal is the sum of an even and an odd part. Even × even and odd × odd are even; even × odd is odd. An odd signal integrates to zero over $[-a, a]$.

study.title: Energy and power
study.body:
Energy and power are defined as if $x$ were a voltage across 1 Ω.
- **Energy signal:** $0 < E < \infty$, so $P = 0$ (pulses, decaying exponentials).
- **Power signal:** $0 < P < \infty$, so $E = \infty$ (periodic signals, $u(t)$).
- For a periodic signal, average over one period: $A\cos(\omega t+\phi)$ has $P = A^2/2$. Some signals ($e^{t}$, $t$) are neither.
Power: $P = \lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_{-T/2}^{T/2} |x(t)|^2 dt$.

study.title: Shift, scale and reverse
study.body:
$x(t - t_0)$ is $x$ delayed (moved right) by $t_0$. $x(at)$ is compressed by $|a|$ for $|a|>1$ and stretched for $|a|<1$. $x(-t)$ is mirrored about $t = 0$.
**Pitfall:** $x(2t-1) = x\big(2(t-\tfrac12)\big)$ is compressed by 2 and then shifted by $\tfrac12$, not by 1.

study.title: Explore: x(at − b)
study.body: Drag $|a|$ and $b$, flip the sign of $a$, and compare the red $x(at-b)$ with the grey $x(t)$. $|a| > 1$ compresses, $|a| < 1$ stretches, a negative $a$ mirrors. The shift is $b/a$, not $b$: the corner of $x$ at $t = 0$ lands where $at - b = 0$, i.e. at $t = b/a$ (readout).

study.title: Mapping key points
study.body: The quickest way to sketch $y(t) = x(at-b)$: a feature of $x$ at $t = t_1$ (a corner, a jump, a peak) appears in $y$ where the argument equals $t_1$. Map every corner of $x$ this way and join the dots. Example: a jump of $x$ at $t_1 = 3$ appears in $x(2t-1)$ at $t = 2$. Time scaling also scales energy: $x(at)$ has energy $E_x/|a|$, while shifting changes nothing.
study.formula: a t - b = t_1 \;\Rightarrow\; t = \frac{t_1 + b}{a}

steps.title: Continuous and discrete time
steps.body: A **continuous-time** signal $x(t)$ has a value at every instant $t$. A **discrete-time** signal $x[n]$ is a sequence: it exists only at integer $n$. Sampling every $T_s$ seconds turns $x(t)$ into $x[n] = x(nT_s)$. Below, the dashed curve is $x(t)$ and the stems are its samples.

steps.prompt: $x(t) = \cos(2\pi\cdot {{f}}\,t)$ with $t$ in s is sampled every $T_s$ = {{Ts|s}}. Which sequence is $x[n] = x(nT_s)$?
steps.explanation: Replace $t$ by $nT_s$: $x[n] = \cos(2\pi f T_s n) = \cos(2\pi\cdot{{f}}\cdot{{Ts}}\,n) = \cos({{2*f*Ts}}\pi n)$. The discrete frequency $\Omega = \omega T_s$ = {{2*f*Ts}}π rad/sample.

steps.title: Periodic signals
steps.body: A signal is **periodic** if it repeats: $x(t + T) = x(t)$ for all $t$. The smallest such $T > 0$ is the **fundamental period** $T_0$. A sinusoid $A\cos(\omega t + \phi)$ has $T_0 = 2\pi/\omega$; the amplitude and phase do not matter.

steps.prompt: Find the fundamental period of $x(t) = {{A}}\cos({{w}}t + \pi/4)$, with $t$ in seconds.
steps.explanation: Only $\omega$ matters: $T_0 = 2\pi/\omega = 2\pi/{{w}}$ = {{2*pi/w|s}}. Amplitude {{A}} and phase $\pi/4$ do not change the period.

steps.title: Shifting and scaling time
steps.body: $x(t - t_0)$ is $x$ delayed by $t_0$ (moved right). $x(at)$ with $a > 1$ is compressed. $x(-t)$ is mirrored. For $x(2t-1)$ (red) find where the argument hits the corners of $x$: $2t - 1 = -1 \Rightarrow t = 0$, and $2t-1 = 2 \Rightarrow t = 1.5$.

steps.prompt: $x(t)$ is nonzero only for $0 \le t \le {{L}}$. For which interval is $y(t) = x({{a}}t - {{b}})$ nonzero?
steps.explanation: $y$ is nonzero where its argument lies in $[0, {{L}}]$: $0 \le {{a}}t - {{b}} \le {{L}}$, so ${{b}}/{{a}} \le t \le ({{L}}+{{b}})/{{a}}$, i.e. ${{b/a}} \le t \le {{(L+b)/a}}$. Scaling and then shifting by the full {{b}} is the classic mistake: the shift is $b/a$.

steps.title: Even and odd signals
steps.body: **Even:** $x(-t) = x(t)$, symmetric about the vertical axis (e.g. $\cos t$, $t^2$). **Odd:** $x(-t) = -x(t)$, symmetric about the origin (e.g. $\sin t$, $t^3$). Any signal splits into an even and an odd part:

steps.prompt: Which signal is **odd**?
steps.explanation: $\sin(-3t) = -\sin(3t)$, so it is odd. $\cos(t)+1$ and $t^2$ are even, and $t\sin t$ is odd × odd = even.

steps.title: Energy and power signals
steps.body: Treat $x(t)$ as a voltage across 1 Ω. A pulse or decaying exponential has finite **energy** $E$ (and zero average power). A periodic signal never dies out, so its energy is infinite, but its average **power** $P$ is finite. For a periodic signal, $P = \frac{1}{T_0}\int_{T_0}|x(t)|^2dt$.

steps.prompt: Classify each signal.
steps.explanation:
- $e^{-2t}u(t)$: $E = \int_0^\infty e^{-4t}dt = 1/4$, finite.
- $5\cos(10t)$: periodic, $P = 5^2/2 = 12.5$.
- $u(t)$: $E = \infty$, but $P = \tfrac12$ (it is 1 for half of a long symmetric window).
- $e^{t}$ grows without bound, so both $E$ and $P$ are infinite.

steps.prompt: Find the fundamental period of $x(t) = \cos(2\pi\cdot{{m*f0}}\,t)$ $+ \sin(2\pi\cdot{{n*f0}}\,t)$ ($t$ in s).
steps.explanation: The frequencies are {{m*f0}} Hz and {{n*f0}} Hz. Their greatest common divisor is $f_0$ = {{f0}} Hz ({{m*f0}} = {{m}}·{{f0}}, {{n*f0}} = {{n}}·{{f0}}). So $T_0 = 1/f_0$ = {{1/f0|s}}: exactly {{m}} periods of the first and {{n}} of the second term.

steps.prompt: Is $x(t) = \cos(2t) + \sin(\pi t)$ periodic?
steps.explanation: The periods are $T_1 = 2\pi/2 = \pi$ s and $T_2 = 2\pi/\pi = 2$ s. Their ratio $\pi/2$ is irrational, so no common multiple exists and the sum never repeats exactly.

steps.prompt: Find the fundamental period $N_0$ (in samples) of $x[n] = \cos\left(\frac{ {{m}}\pi n}{ {{N/2}} }\right)$.
steps.explanation: Write $\Omega_0/2\pi = \frac{ {{m}}\pi/{{N/2}} }{2\pi} = \frac{ {{m}} }{ {{N}} }$. This fraction is already in lowest terms, so $N_0$ = {{N}} samples (in that time the cosine goes through {{m}} full cycles).

steps.prompt: $x[n] = \cos(0.5n)$ is periodic.
steps.explanation: $\Omega_0/2\pi = 0.5/2\pi = 1/(4\pi)$ is irrational, so no integer $N$ gives $0.5N = 2\pi k$. Unlike $\cos(0.5t)$, the sequence never repeats exactly.

steps.prompt: Find the energy of $x(t) = {{A}}e^{-{{a}}t}u(t)$ ($x$ in V, $t$ in s, energy into 1 Ω).
Find the energy of the triangular pulse shown ($x$ in V, $t$ in s, energy into 1 Ω).
steps.explanation: The graph gives height $A$ = {{A}} V and half-width $T$ = {{T}} s. By symmetry, $E = 2\int_0^T \left(\frac{A t}{T}\right)^2dt = \frac{2A^2T}{3} = \frac{2\cdot{{A^2}}\cdot{{T}}}{3}$ = {{2*A^2*T/3|J}}. (Not $A^2\cdot 2T$: the square of a ramp is not the ramp.)

steps.prompt: Find the average power of $x(t) = {{D}} + {{A}}\cos({{w}}t)$ (into 1 Ω).
steps.explanation: The cross term $2DA\cos(\omega t)$ averages to zero, so $P = D^2 + \frac{A^2}{2} = {{D^2}} + {{A^2/2}}$ = {{D^2+A^2/2|W}}.

steps.prompt: The periodic pulse train shown is a voltage across 1 Ω. Find its average power.
steps.explanation: From the graph: amplitude $A$ = {{A}} V, pulse width $\tau$ = {{tau|s}}, period $T$ = {{T|s}}. Over one period, $P = \frac{1}{T}\int_0^{\tau}A^2dt = A^2\frac{\tau}{T} = {{A^2}}\cdot{{tau/T}}$ = {{A^2*tau/T|W}}.

steps.prompt: Find the even part $x_e(t)$ at $t = {{t0}}$ for $x(t) = {{p}} + {{q}}t + {{r}}t^2 + {{s}}t^3$.
The graph shows $x(t)$. Which graph is $y(t) = x(2t - 1)$?
steps.explanation: Map the corners: $x$ jumps up at $t=-1$, starts ramping down at $t = 0$ and reaches 0 at $t = 2$. Solve $2t - 1 = -1, 0, 2$: $t = 0,\ 0.5,\ 1.5$. So $y$ is 1 on $[0, 0.5)$ and ramps down to 0 at $t = 1.5$. The other graphs are $x(2t-2)$, $x(2t+1)$ and $x(t-1)$.

steps.prompt: Same $x(t)$ as shown. Which graph is $y(t) = x(1 - t)$?
steps.explanation: $x(1-t) = x\big(-(t-1)\big)$: mirror $x$, then delay by 1. Corners: $1 - t = -1, 0, 2$ give $t = 2,\ 1,\ -1$. So $y$ ramps up from 0 at $t=-1$ to 1 at $t = 1$ and stays 1 until $t = 2$. The others are $x(-t-1)$, $x(t-1)$ and $x(-t)$.

steps.prompt: $x(t)$ has a single peak, at $t = {{t1}}$.
steps.explanation: The peak is where the argument equals {{t1}}.

ask.prompt: At what time $t$ does $y(t) = x({{a}}t - {{b}})$ peak?
ask.explanation: Set the argument equal to the peak position: ${{a}}t - {{b}} = {{t1}} \Rightarrow t = \frac{ {{t1}} + {{b}} }{ {{a}} }$ = {{t0}} s.

ask.prompt: At what time $t$ does $y(t) = x({{b}} - {{a}}t)$ peak?
ask.explanation: Set the argument equal to the peak position: ${{b}} - {{a}}t = {{t1}} \Rightarrow t = \frac{ {{b}} - ({{t1}}) }{ {{a}} }$ = {{t0r}} s. The reversal mirrors the signal, so the peak can move to the other side.

steps.require: min(3.8 - max(abs((bt-1)/at), abs(bt/at), abs((bt+2)/at)), abs(at-1) + abs(bt))
steps.prompt: The grey curve is $x(t)$. Set $a$ and $b$ so that the red $y(t) = x(at - b)$ lies exactly on the dashed orange target.
steps.hint: Map two corners of $x$: a corner at $t_1$ appears where $at - b = t_1$.
steps.explanation: The target is $x({{at}}t - ({{bt}}))$. Corners of $x$: the jump at $t = -1$, the start of the ramp at $t = 0$ and its end at $t = 2$. They land where ${{at}}t - ({{bt}})$ equals $-1$, 0 and 2: $t$ = {{(bt-1)/at}}, {{bt/at}} and {{(bt+2)/at}}. Here $|a|$ = {{abs(at)}}: $|a| > 1$ compresses, $|a| < 1$ stretches, and a negative $a$ mirrors, so the ramp then runs the other way.

steps.prompt: The sequence $x[n]$ is shown (zero outside $0 \le n \le 4$). Let $y[n] = x[{{c}} - n]$. Find $y[{{c-j}}]$.
$x(t)$ has energy $E_x$ = {{E}} J. Find the energy of $y(t) = {{K}}\,x({{a}}t - {{b}})$.
steps.explanation: The shift by {{b}} changes nothing. Compressing by {{a}} divides the energy by {{a}} ($\int |x(at)|^2dt = \frac{1}{a}\int|x(\tau)|^2d\tau$). The gain {{K}} multiplies it by {{K^2}}. So $E_y = \frac{ {{K^2}}\cdot{{E}} }{ {{a}} }$ = {{K^2*E/a|J}}.

steps.prompt: $x(t) = \frac{t}{2}$ for $0 \le t < 2$ and 0 elsewhere (a ramp up to 1). Which graph is its **even part** $x_e(t)$?
steps.explanation: $x_e(t) = \frac12[x(t) + x(-t)]$. For $0<t<2$ only $x(t) = t/2$ contributes, giving $t/4$; for $-2<t<0$ only $x(-t)$ contributes, giving $|t|/4$. So $x_e$ is a V shape reaching 0.5 at $t = \pm2$. The others are the odd part, $x(t) + x(-t)$ without the ½, and $x(-t)$.

steps.prompt: Order the operations that turn $x(t)$ into $y(t) = x(-2t + 4)$.
steps.explanation: Each step replaces $t$ in the previous result: $x(t)\to x(t+4)$, then $t \to 2t$ gives $x(2t + 4)$, then $t \to -t$ gives $x(-2t+4)$. Check: the value $x(0)$ appears at $-2t + 4 = 0$, i.e. $t = 2$.

steps.prompt: If $x(t)$ is periodic with average power $P$, then $y(t) = x(3t)$ has average power $3P$.
steps.explanation: $y$ is $x$ compressed by 3: its period is $T_0/3$, but one period of $y$ contains exactly the same values, just faster. $P = \frac{1}{T_0/3}\int_0^{T_0/3}|x(3t)|^2dt = \frac{1}{T_0}\int_0^{T_0}|x(\tau)|^2d\tau$, the same $P$. (Energy signals are different: there $E$ is divided by 3.)

steps.prompt: The product of two odd signals is odd.
steps.explanation: If $x_1(-t) = -x_1(t)$ and $x_2(-t) = -x_2(t)$, then $x_1(-t)x_2(-t) = (-x_1)(-x_2) = x_1(t)x_2(t)$: the product is **even**. Example: $t\cdot\sin t$.
